I can see a few different possibilities.

  1. Embrace, Extend, Extinguish. This is not out of the question, and it seems that, if this is Microsoft's strategy, offering Linux compatibility is one part of a two-pronged strategy (the other involving their attempts to get deeply involved in Android development and apps). If they can get away with it they may want the standard way to run Linux apps to be as a subsystem for Windows 10, where using the Linux kernel is generally reserved for specialized applications or low-end things. In this case it's going to get much more aggressive in the near future in all likelihood. Something important to remember is that Microsoft recently got the DoJ off their backs for monopolist tendencies. Many Voat users aren't aware of this, but Microsoft was extremely bad and did nasty things back in the mid-late 90s. In this scenario Microsoft intends to make up for lost time, and do so much damage that another court case against them won't matter to a bunch of corpses that were once competition.

  2. Absorption. I read an interesting article about this, but I can't find it, so I'm going with what I recall off the top of my head and my own thoughts on the subject. In this case, Windows 10 is attempting to harness all of the goodies on Linux. IIRC the portions of Ubuntu being ported are, at first, not only going to not include the Linux kernel, but won't offer graphical support, either. This makes it possible for Windows 10 to run Linux-based applications and servers that are command-line only, but have lackluster or non-existent Windows ports. Essentially they try to tame Linux by making it a subsystem, and make it an option for Windows. This allows companies to think that they're getting a worse bargain for not having Windows, because (or so they assume) they're getting everything from Linux in the Windows package for free.

  3. Abandon Ship. Microsoft sees the future is tablets and smart phones. They don't seem to care they have a lock on the desktop market, which will be useful for many years to come and probably has innovation in it yet, but want to jump on the new, exciting, shiny stuff. Note that Microsoft is partnering with not only Canonical, but Red Hat. These are giants in the Linux ecosystem. And Microsoft's biggest thing is beyond OS's - it's about cloud computing. And all of that is based on Red Hat Linux. They see no future for Windows in the long run, especially given its failure to seize the tablet and phone market, the rather sound rejection of Windows 8, and the failure of the Windows Store. In this scenario, the spyware in Windows 10 becomes particularly interesting since they may try to leverage it in one way or another as they try to shape their cloud business, especially if they try to lure in home consumers so that everyday people just by Microsoft dumb terminals that run off of a system MS controls. I would say that a large portion of the evidence of this one is (as someone else in this thread pointed out) they already consider Win32, the crown jewels of Windows compatibility, to be "legacy," even though all of their new fancy frameworks sooner or later boil down to Win32 or Win64.

Personally I think it's #1 at first with a fallback to #2. I kind of hope it's #3, though, I've been rooting for Linux for quite some time, and Microsoft's love of spyware is extremely invasive.
